title: Testing
description: Write tests that catch real bugs without slowing you down: unit tests with Vitest and Jest, component tests with React Testing Library, network mocking with MSW, API tests with supertest and end-to-end tests with Playwright.

chapters.title: Why We Test: Pyramid, Trophy and What to Test
chapters.summary: Understand the kinds of automated tests, how the testing pyramid and testing trophy allocate effort, and how to decide what is worth testing.

lesson.heading: What automated tests are for
lesson.body:
Tests are code that checks other code. Their real value is **confidence to change things**: refactor, upgrade dependencies and ship on a Friday without manually clicking through the app. A good test suite catches regressions before users do, documents intended behavior and makes code review faster because reviewers can trust the checks.

Tests also have costs: writing time, maintenance when code changes, CI minutes, and the damage done by flaky tests that fail randomly and train people to ignore red builds. The goal is not maximum test count; it is the most confidence per unit of cost.

A useful rule from Kent C. Dodds: "The more your tests resemble the way your software is used, the more confidence they can give you."

lesson.heading: The kinds of tests
lesson.body:
- **Static analysis**: TypeScript, ESLint. Catches typos, wrong types and unsafe patterns without running code. Cheapest of all.
- **Unit tests**: one function, hook or small component in isolation, dependencies mocked. Very fast (milliseconds), precise failure messages.
- **Integration tests**: several units working together, for example a form component with its validation, state and a mocked network layer, or an API route with a real database. Slower, much more realistic.
- **End-to-end (E2E) tests**: drive a real browser against a running app, through the UI, often with a real backend. Highest confidence per test, slowest, most likely to flake.
- Others: contract tests (API producer and consumer agree on a schema), visual regression tests (screenshot diffs), accessibility checks (axe), performance budgets, manual exploratory testing.

lesson.heading: Pyramid vs trophy
lesson.body:
The **testing pyramid** (Mike Cohn) says: many unit tests at the base, fewer integration tests, very few E2E tests at the top, because higher tests are slower and more expensive.

The **testing trophy** (Kent C. Dodds) adapts this for modern frontend work: a base of static analysis, a small layer of unit tests, the **largest layer of integration tests**, and a cap of E2E tests. The argument: frontend bugs usually live in how pieces fit together (props, state, effects, network), and tools like React Testing Library and MSW make integration tests nearly as fast as unit tests.

Both agree on the essential point: E2E tests are valuable but should cover critical user journeys (sign up, checkout, login), not every edge case. Edge cases belong in cheaper, faster layers.

lesson.heading: Test behavior, not implementation
lesson.body:
A test should fail when the behavior breaks and pass when you refactor without changing behavior. Tests coupled to implementation details produce two problems: **false negatives** (they break on a harmless refactor) and **false positives** (they pass even though the user-facing behavior is broken).

Implementation details include component state variable names, internal method calls, CSS class names and the exact component tree. Behavior is what users and callers observe: rendered text and roles, events fired, network requests made, return values.

Good test anatomy is Arrange, Act, Assert (or Given, When, Then): set up the situation, perform one action, check the outcome. One behavior per test, a name that describes it ("shows an error when the email is invalid"), and no logic like loops or conditionals in the test body.

lesson.heading: Deciding what to test
lesson.body:
Prioritize by risk and value:

- Business-critical paths: payments, auth, data loss, anything that costs money or trust when broken
- Complex logic: calculations, parsing, state machines, permission rules
- Code that has broken before: every bug fix gets a regression test that fails without the fix
- Public contracts: API responses, shared library functions, component props used across the app

Skip or minimize: trivial getters, third-party library internals, framework behavior, and pure layout markup with no logic. Snapshot tests of large component trees are usually low value: they break on every change and reviewers approve updates without reading them. Small, focused inline snapshots of serialized data can be fine.

keyPoints: Tests buy confidence to change code; measure value as confidence per cost, not test count.
Static analysis, unit, integration and E2E tests trade speed and precision for realism.
The pyramid favors many unit tests; the trophy favors integration tests for frontend code.
Use E2E tests for critical user journeys, not for every edge case.
Test observable behavior so refactors do not break tests and real bugs do.
Structure tests as Arrange, Act, Assert with one behavior per test.
Every bug fix should come with a regression test that fails without the fix.

questions.prompt: In the testing trophy, which layer is meant to be the largest?
questions.explanation: The trophy argues integration tests give the best balance of confidence and cost for UI code, because most frontend bugs come from how pieces work together.

questions.prompt: A test fails after you rename a private state variable in a component, though the UI behaves identically. What kind of problem is this?
options: A false negative caused by testing implementation details
questions.explanation: The behavior did not change, but the test did fail. Tests coupled to internals produce this noise and discourage refactoring.

questions.prompt: Which is the best candidate for an E2E test?
options: Every validation message on the signup form
The full checkout flow from cart to order confirmation
The color of a disabled button
questions.explanation: E2E tests are slow and costly, so they should cover critical user journeys across the whole stack. Validation messages and helpers are cheaper to cover with integration and unit tests.

questions.prompt: Which kind of check is cheapest and catches a misspelled property on a typed object before any test runs?
questions.explanation: Static analysis runs in the editor and CI without executing code, catching whole classes of bugs for nearly zero cost. It is the base of the trophy.

questions.prompt: You fixed a bug where discounts were applied twice. What should you add?
options: A snapshot of the cart component
A regression test that fails without the fix and passes with it
An E2E test of the whole site
questions.explanation: A regression test proves the fix works and prevents the same bug returning. Writing it first and watching it fail confirms it actually reproduces the bug.

questions.prompt: What does the Arrange, Act, Assert pattern describe?
options: The order of CI pipeline stages
Setting up state, performing an action, then checking the outcome
questions.explanation: AAA keeps each test readable: given a situation, when something happens, then expect a result.

questions.prompt: Large snapshot tests of whole component trees are a reliable way to catch regressions.
questions.explanation: They fail on every markup change, so developers update them with `-u` without reading the diff. They rarely express intended behavior. Targeted assertions are more useful.

questions.prompt: Tests that resemble how users interact with the software generally give more confidence.
questions.explanation: If a test interacts the way a user does (roles, labels, clicks, typing), passing it means users can likely do the same. This is the guiding principle of Testing Library.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which are implementation details a component test should usually avoid asserting on?
options: CSS class names used for styling
Whether an internal helper function was called
The network request the component sends
questions.explanation: Users never see state, class names or private helpers. Visible output and outgoing requests are observable behavior and fair to assert.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: the testing ___ puts many unit tests at the base and few E2E tests at the top.
questions.explanation: Mike Cohn's pyramid reflects that lower-level tests are faster and cheaper; the trophy is a later variation focused on integration.

questions.prompt: Explain the testing pyramid and the testing trophy. How would you apply them to a React application?
questions.answer: The pyramid says to have many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests and very few slow E2E tests. The trophy, from Kent C. Dodds, keeps the idea that E2E is expensive but makes integration tests the largest layer, adds static analysis at the base, and shrinks pure unit tests. For a React app I would follow the trophy: TypeScript and ESLint everywhere, unit tests for pure logic like pricing or date utils, integration tests with React Testing Library and MSW for features (render a page or feature, interact like a user, mock only the network), and a handful of Playwright tests for critical journeys like login and checkout. The reasoning is that most frontend bugs come from wiring between components, state and APIs, which integration tests catch cheaply.

questions.prompt: What makes a test good? What makes one bad?
questions.answer:
- Good: it fails when behavior breaks and only then, so it survives refactors.
- Good: it is readable as a specification, with a descriptive name, clear Arrange-Act-Assert and one behavior per test.
- Good: it is fast, deterministic and isolated, with no dependence on order, time or shared state.
- Good: failure messages point straight at the problem.
- Bad: asserting internals (state, private methods, class names), so it breaks on refactors.
- Bad: over-mocking, so it passes while the real integration is broken.
- Bad: flaky timing with arbitrary sleeps, giant snapshots nobody reads, logic and loops in tests, and tests that test the framework rather than our code.

questions.prompt: You join a team with zero tests on a large frontend. Where do you start?
questions.answer: I would not try to backfill coverage everywhere. First, set up the tooling and CI (Vitest, React Testing Library, MSW, Playwright) so writing a test is easy, and turn on TypeScript strictness and ESLint, the cheapest wins. Next, add a few E2E smoke tests for the most critical journeys (login, core workflow, payment) so the biggest risks are covered quickly. Then adopt a rule going forward: every bug fix gets a regression test and every new feature ships with integration tests. Finally, add tests around risky areas before refactoring them. Coverage grows where change actually happens, which is where tests pay off.
